# Opamma Saṁyutta (SN 20)
**ID:** SN 20
**Section:** Saṁyuttanikāya (sn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Opamma Saṁyutta
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/sn20

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Opamma Saṁyutta* ("Linked Discourses with Similes", SN 20) is the twentieth collection of the *Saṁyuttanikāya*, situated as the ninth chapter of the *Nidānavagga* [Bodhi 2003; SuttaCentral]. While most saṁyuttas in the canon are organized by specific doctrinal topics, interlocutors, or classes of beings, this collection is distinguished by its structural reliance on vivid parables and extended similes to convey monastic training and spiritual principles [Bodhi 2003; SuttaCentral]. It comprises eleven or twelve suttas addressing diverse subjects [Bodhi 2003; SuttaCentral]. Notable teachings include the roof-peak simile in SN 20.1, illustrating how all unwholesome states converge upon and are rooted in ignorance [Flores 2008; Nyanaponika and Fromm 2000]; the importance of guarded senses and mindfulness, shown by the cat and mouse simile in the *Biḷārasutta* (SN 20.10) [Anālayo 2014]; the power of loving-kindness (*mettā*); the impermanence of life-formations (*āyusaṅkhāra*); and the famous drum-peg simile in the *Āṇisutta* (SN 20.7), which warns against the future neglect of deep discourses connected with emptiness (*suññata-paṭisaṁyutta*) in favor of literary embellishments [Choong 1999; Bodhi 2003].
Curated parallels and DharmaNexus alignments show that the *Opamma Saṁyutta* corresponds directly to a section in the Chinese *Saṁyuktāgama* (preserved largely in T 99, fascicle 47, texts 1252–1262, as well as T 100) [Bodhi 2003; DharmaNexus; SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus also aligns passages with the *Ekottarika Āgama* (T 125), *Madhyama Āgama* (T 26), and the Tibetan *Vinayavastu* [DharmaNexus]. Beyond the Āgamas, early manuscript witnesses exist: a Central Asian Sanskrit manuscript fragment preserves a parallel to the *Satti Sutta* (SN 20.5 / *Śakti-sūtra*) [Saha 1966], while a Gāndhārī birchbark scroll from the Senior collection (RS 22) contains the conclusion of a parallel to the *Dhanuggahasutta* (SN 20.6) on the rapid fleeting of life [Allon, Senior Manuscripts]. Internally, DharmaNexus records substantial textual reuse between SN 20 and other collections, most prominently SN 17, SN 56, and AN 5 [DharmaNexus].
